title: Vascular Conditions
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers disease of the blood vessels themselves: hardening and atherosclerosis of arteries, the inherited lipid disorder that accelerates it, aneurysm and dissection of the aorta, chronic limb ischemia and cholesterol embolism, venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, venous insufficiency, vasospasm, and the vasculitides. Board questions usually give a patient's age, sex, exposures, and the pattern of vessels involved, then ask for the lesion, the mechanism, or the complication. Most of these questions can be solved from three ideas: which layer of the wall fails, what size of vessel is affected, and how flow, pressure, and wall tension change as a result.
prerequisites: Layers of the arterial and venous wall (intima, media, adventitia) and vasa vasorum
Hemodynamics: pressure, flow, resistance, and the law of Laplace (CV-11)
Lipoprotein classes, the LDL receptor, and cholesterol homeostasis (CV-13)
Hypersensitivity types II, III, and IV and the role of neutrophils and T cells

connections.how: Coronary atherosclerosis and plaque rupture are the substrate for angina and myocardial infarction.
Raised pressure drives arteriolosclerosis, accelerates atherosclerosis, and is the main risk factor for aortic dissection.
Pulmonary embolism produces hypoxemia through ventilation-perfusion mismatch, which the alveolar-arterial gradient detects.
Arteriolosclerosis, atheroemboli, polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA vasculitis, and IgA vasculitis each injure the kidney in a distinct pattern.
Polymyalgia rheumatica, systemic sclerosis, lupus, Marfan syndrome, and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome all present through the vessels.

terms.def: Thickening and loss of elasticity of arterial walls; the umbrella term for atherosclerosis, arteriolosclerosis, and medial calcific sclerosis.
An intimal plaque with a lipid-rich necrotic core covered by a fibrous cap of smooth muscle cells and collagen.
A macrophage or smooth muscle cell filled with lipid droplets after taking up modified LDL through scavenger receptors.
A localized permanent dilation of a vessel or the heart involving all layers of the wall (true) or contained by adventitia or clot (false).
Entry of blood through an intimal tear into the media, splitting the wall and creating a false lumen.
Ankle systolic pressure divided by brachial systolic pressure; normal about 1.00 to 1.40.
The three conditions that favor thrombosis: stasis or turbulent flow, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability.
The difference between calculated alveolar PO2 and measured arterial PO2; it widens when gas exchange is impaired.
Inflammation of the vessel wall, classified by the size of vessel mainly affected and by immune mechanism.
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, mainly against proteinase 3 (PR3) or myeloperoxidase (MPO), that activate neutrophils against small vessels.
Describing vasculitis or glomerulonephritis with little or no immunoglobulin or complement deposited in the lesion, typical of ANCA disease.

blocks.text: Arteriosclerosis means hardening of the arteries: the wall thickens and loses elasticity. It takes three patterns that differ in the size of vessel, the layer affected, and whether the lumen narrows. Keeping them apart matters because only two of the three reduce flow.

Atherosclerosis is an intimal disease of elastic and large to medium muscular arteries, in which lipid, inflammatory cells, and fibrous tissue form plaques that bulge into the lumen (C02). Arteriolosclerosis affects small arteries and arterioles. In the hyaline form, plasma proteins leak across injured endothelium and smooth muscle cells lay down excess matrix, giving a homogeneous pink, glassy wall. It accompanies aging, long-standing benign hypertension, and diabetes; in the kidney it causes nephrosclerosis with a finely granular cortical surface, and in diabetes it affects both afferent and efferent arterioles. In the hyperplastic form, seen with severe (malignant) hypertension, smooth muscle cells and reduplicated basement membrane form concentric onion-skin layers, often with fibrinoid necrosis of the wall, and the narrowed lumen produces renal ischemia with pinpoint cortical hemorrhages.

Monckeberg medial calcific sclerosis is calcification of the media of medium muscular arteries, typically the femoral, tibial, radial, and ulnar arteries, in people over about 50. The calcium is deposited in the media and internal elastic lamina, so the intima and lumen are spared and flow is not reduced. The calcified vessel appears as a pipestem on radiographs and is palpably hard. It matters diagnostically: a stiff artery resists cuff compression, so ankle pressure reads falsely high and the ankle-brachial index can exceed 1.40 (C06), which is common in diabetes and chronic kidney disease.

sections.title: Pathogenesis, distribution, and complications of atherosclerosis

blocks.text: Atherosclerosis is best understood as a chronic inflammatory response of the arterial wall to endothelial injury. Endothelial dysfunction develops at branch points and curvatures, where flow is disturbed rather than laminar, and is promoted by hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia, and inflammation. The dysfunctional endothelium becomes more permeable and expresses adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1, so LDL and monocytes enter the intima.

blocks.title: From endothelial injury to complicated plaque
steps: Endothelial dysfunction at branch points and curvatures
LDL enters the intima and is oxidized
Monocytes adhere, migrate in, become macrophages
Scavenger receptor uptake of oxidized LDL: foam cells
Fatty streak: flat intimal collection of foam cells
PDGF and other growth factors recruit smooth muscle from the media
Fibrous cap of collagen over a necrotic lipid core
Rupture, erosion, hemorrhage, or calcification: complicated plaque
blocks.caption: Scavenger receptors are not down-regulated by cell cholesterol, so macrophages keep taking up oxidized LDL until they become foam cells.

blocks.text: Fatty streaks are present in the aortas of virtually all children over about 10 and are not themselves obstructive. A mature atheroma has a fibrous cap of smooth muscle cells and collagen over a core of lipid, necrotic debris, foam cells, and cholesterol crystals. Plaques are patchy and favor, in descending order, the abdominal aorta (more than the thoracic), the coronary arteries, the popliteal arteries, the internal carotid arteries, and the circle of Willis. Major modifiable risks are smoking, hypertension, raised LDL, and diabetes; fixed risks are age, male sex, and family history.

The danger of a plaque depends more on its stability than its size. A vulnerable plaque has a thin cap, a large lipid core, and many inflammatory cells: macrophage metalloproteinases digest collagen and T cell interferon gamma suppresses smooth muscle collagen synthesis. When the cap ruptures, exposed tissue factor and collagen trigger thrombosis, which is why many myocardial infarctions arise from plaques that were not severely stenotic. A stable plaque narrows the lumen gradually; once a stenosis reaches about 70%, flow can no longer rise to meet demand and ischemia appears with exertion.

blocks.title: Complications of atherosclerosis
rows: Slow plaque growth limits flow reserve
Stable angina, claudication, renal artery stenosis
Cap disruption exposes tissue factor and collagen
Plaque debris or thrombus breaks off downstream
Atheroemboli to kidney and toes; carotid emboli to brain
Intimal plaque starves and weakens the underlying media
Rupture of plaque microvessels expands it abruptly
blocks.caption: Thrombosis on a disrupted plaque causes most acute events; stenosis causes chronic demand ischemia.

blocks.predict: A 58-year-old with a 40% coronary stenosis on a recent angiogram suffers an acute myocardial infarction in that artery. How can a modest stenosis cause an infarct?
blocks.explain: The event depends on plaque stability, not size: a lipid-rich plaque with a thin, inflamed cap can rupture and expose thrombogenic contents, and the overlying thrombus occludes the vessel.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on vulnerable plaque and the complications table.

blocks.text: Hepatic LDL receptors bind apolipoprotein B-100 on LDL and remove it from plasma by clathrin-mediated endocytosis. The cholesterol released in the lysosome keeps SREBP-2 inactive in the endoplasmic reticulum, which lowers the synthesis of HMG-CoA reductase and of new LDL receptors. Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is an autosomal dominant failure of this clearance, most often from loss-of-function mutations in the LDL receptor gene (LDLR), less often in APOB (receptor binding site) or from gain-of-function mutations in PCSK9, a protein that steers the receptor to lysosomal degradation.

Because clearance falls while the liver, sensing less cholesterol, keeps synthesizing it, plasma LDL rises in proportion to the receptor defect. Heterozygotes, about 1 in 250 people, have roughly half the normal receptor activity and LDL often above 190 mg/dL from childhood; coronary disease commonly appears in the fourth to fifth decade in men and somewhat later in women. Homozygotes have little or no receptor activity, LDL often above 500 mg/dL, and coronary disease or myocardial infarction in childhood or the teens. Triglycerides are usually normal, which separates FH from combined hyperlipidemias.

The physical findings are deposits of LDL-derived cholesterol taken up by macrophages. Tendon xanthomas are firm nodules in the Achilles tendon and the extensor tendons of the hands and are highly suggestive of FH. Xanthelasma (yellow plaques on the eyelids) and corneal arcus (a gray-white ring at the corneal margin) are less specific because both occur in older adults with normal lipids; arcus before about age 45 suggests FH. Homozygotes may also have planar cutaneous xanthomas and lipid deposits in the aortic root and valve. The same receptor-macrophage process in the arterial intima drives premature atherosclerosis (C02).

blocks.title: Heterozygous versus homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
rows: Rare, about 1 in several hundred thousand
Premature, often fourth to fifth decade
Same plus planar cutaneous xanthomas in childhood
blocks.caption: Gene dosage sets the LDL level and the age at which atherosclerosis becomes clinical.

sections.title: Aneurysms: abdominal, thoracic, berry, and mycotic

blocks.text: An aneurysm forms when the media can no longer bear wall stress, because its elastin, collagen, or smooth muscle has been lost or weakened. A true aneurysm involves all three layers; a false aneurysm (pseudoaneurysm) is a leak contained by adventitia or clot, often at an arterial puncture or graft anastomosis. Once a segment dilates, the law of Laplace makes it worse: wall stress is proportional to pressure times radius divided by wall thickness, so a wider, thinner segment carries more stress and enlarges faster.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), a dilation to 3 cm or more, is the most common aortic aneurysm. It is associated with atherosclerosis and is typical of men over 60 who smoke, with hypertension and family history as added risks. It usually lies below the renal arteries, where the media has few vasa vasorum and a thick plaque impairs diffusion of nutrients to it, while inflammation and matrix metalloproteinases degrade the matrix. Most are silent and found as a pulsatile abdominal mass or on imaging. Rupture risk rises steeply with diameter, from very low below 4 cm to high above about 5.5 cm, and presents with abdominal or back pain, hypotension, and a pulsatile mass.

Thoracic aortic aneurysms usually reflect cystic medial degeneration (loss of elastic fibers and smooth muscle with pools of ground substance) from hypertension or connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome. Tertiary syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum of the ascending aorta, giving medial ischemia, a wrinkled tree-bark intima, and dilation of the aortic root with aortic regurgitation. Both can compress mediastinal structures, causing cough, dysphagia, or hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve stretch.

Aortic root dilation and regurgitation; compression; dissection

blocks.title: Why large aneurysms rupture faster
blocks.text: Wall stress is about pressure times radius divided by wall thickness. Compare a normal infrarenal aorta of 2 cm diameter (radius 1 cm) with a 6 cm aneurysm (radius 3 cm) at the same blood pressure. Radius has tripled, so stress has tripled even before the wall thins. As the aneurysm stretches, its wall becomes thinner, which raises stress further. Higher stress speeds degradation of the remaining matrix, which allows more dilation. This positive feedback explains why expansion accelerates as diameter grows and why rupture risk climbs steeply above about 5.5 cm. Hypertension raises the pressure term and adds to every step.

In aortic dissection, blood enters the media through an intimal tear and splits the wall along its length, creating a false lumen. The underlying problem is a weakened media. Hypertension, present in most patients, causes medial degeneration and raises the shear and wall stress that drive the split. Younger patients usually have a connective tissue defect: cystic medial degeneration in Marfan syndrome (defective fibrillin-1 and excess TGF-beta signaling), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, bicuspid aortic valve with its associated aortopathy, or Turner syndrome (often with bicuspid valve and coarctation). Abrupt surges in pressure, as with cocaine or the hemodynamic load of pregnancy, can also trigger it. Heavy atherosclerosis or medial scarring tends to stop a dissection from spreading, so dissection is not a typical complication of atherosclerosis.

blocks.title: Consequences of a proximal dissection
steps: Weakened media plus high wall stress
Intimal tear, usually in the ascending aorta
Blood splits the media: false lumen
Proximal spread: aortic root, valve support lost, regurgitation
Rupture into pericardium: hemopericardium and tamponade
Branch compression: coronary, carotid, subclavian, renal, mesenteric ischemia
External rupture: hemothorax or exsanguination
blocks.caption: Outward rupture, into the pericardium, pleural cavity, or peritoneum, is the usual cause of death.

blocks.text: The pain is sudden, severe, and tearing or ripping, felt in the anterior chest and radiating to the back between the scapulae as the dissection advances. If the false lumen narrows a subclavian artery, the pulse is weak and the blood pressure is lower in that arm, giving unequal arm pressures. The chest radiograph may show a widened mediastinum. A new diastolic murmur indicates aortic regurgitation from root dilation; hypotension with distended neck veins suggests tamponade; neurologic deficits, paraplegia, oliguria, or abdominal pain indicate branch occlusion.

Hypertension; younger patients with Marfan or bicuspid valve
Highest: tamponade, aortic regurgitation, coronary occlusion
Does not involve the ascending aorta; usually begins beyond the left subclavian artery
Lower; complications mainly branch ischemia and rupture
blocks.caption: The ascending aorta decides the type because its involvement threatens the valve, pericardium, and coronary arteries.

blocks.predict: A 32-year-old tall man with long fingers develops tearing chest pain, then hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds. What has happened?
blocks.explain: A Stanford A dissection in Marfan syndrome has ruptured back into the pericardium, causing tamponade that limits ventricular filling.

sections.title: Peripheral arterial disease and atheroembolic disease

blocks.text: Peripheral arterial disease (PAD) is atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries to the legs, most strongly linked to smoking and diabetes. Its symptoms follow from flow reserve. At rest, a stenosed artery can still deliver enough blood, but during walking the calf arterioles dilate and demand rises while the fixed stenosis prevents flow from increasing. The result is intermittent claudication: cramping pain in the muscle group below the stenosis, reproduced by a set distance of walking and relieved within minutes by rest. Superficial femoral disease causes calf pain; aortoiliac disease causes buttock and thigh pain.

As stenosis worsens, resting flow becomes inadequate. Rest pain in the forefoot, typically at night and eased by hanging the foot down (gravity raises perfusion pressure), signals critical ischemia, followed by nonhealing ulcers on the toes and pressure points and gangrene. Chronic ischemia also produces weak or absent pulses, cool skin, hair loss, thin shiny skin, thickened nails, and dependent rubor with pallor on elevation. Leriche syndrome is occlusion at the aortic bifurcation and causes buttock and thigh claudication, absent or diminished femoral pulses, and erectile dysfunction from reduced internal iliac flow.

blocks.title: Interpreting the ankle-brachial index
rows: Noncompressible calcified arteries (Monckeberg, diabetes, chronic kidney disease); result unreliable
PAD: pressure is lost across stenoses
Severe disease, often with rest pain or tissue loss
blocks.caption: Normally ankle pressure equals or slightly exceeds arm pressure because of pulse wave amplification; a lower ankle pressure means flow has crossed a resistance.

blocks.text: Atheroembolic (cholesterol embolization) disease occurs when an ulcerated plaque in the aorta or a large artery showers cholesterol crystals into small distal arteries. It is classically triggered by arterial catheterization, angiography, or vascular surgery that scrapes a plaque, and occasionally by anticoagulation or thrombolysis. Crystals lodge in arterioles of about 100 to 200 micrometers and incite inflammation, so the patient has blue or purple toes and livedo reticularis with intact pedal pulses, because the large arteries remain open. Kidney involvement causes progressive renal failure, and blood tests may show eosinophilia and low complement. Biopsy shows biconvex, needle-shaped clefts in arterioles where cholesterol crystals were dissolved during tissue processing.

More than 95% of pulmonary emboli arise from thrombi in the deep veins of the leg, especially the proximal veins (popliteal, femoral, and iliac), which are large enough to release sizable clots. A detached thrombus passes through the right heart into the pulmonary arteries. Its effects depend on size and on the patient's cardiopulmonary reserve: a large saddle embolus at the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery can cause sudden death, while small emboli may be silent.

blocks.title: From pulmonary arterial obstruction to signs
steps: Embolus obstructs pulmonary arteries
Pulmonary vascular resistance rises abruptly
Right ventricle dilates and fails: acute cor pulmonale
Blood diverted to open lung units: low V/Q areas
Hypoxemia with widened A-a gradient
Hypoxemia and receptor stimulation drive hyperventilation
Low PaCO2: respiratory alkalosis
blocks.caption: Obstruction of roughly 60% or more of the pulmonary circulation can cause shock or sudden death.

blocks.text: The classic presentation is sudden dyspnea with tachypnea and tachycardia; pleuritic chest pain and hemoptysis suggest a small peripheral embolus that has irritated the pleura or caused infarction. Hypoxemia arises mainly from ventilation-perfusion mismatch: obstructed regions are ventilated but not perfused (dead space), while their blood is redirected to open regions that become overperfused relative to ventilation; local loss of surfactant and atelectasis add shunt. Because alveolar gas is normal or even high in oxygen while arterial PO2 falls, the A-a gradient widens, which separates PE from hypoventilation. Acute right ventricular strain shows as a dilated right ventricle, raised jugular venous pressure, sinus tachycardia (the most common ECG finding), sometimes a new right bundle branch block or an S1Q3T3 pattern, and elevated troponin or BNP. D-dimer, a fibrin degradation product, is sensitive but not specific.

Only about 10% of emboli cause pulmonary infarction. The lung has a dual supply: bronchial arteries from the systemic circulation continue to perfuse the tissue distal to the block, and alveolar oxygen diffuses into the tissue directly. Infarction occurs mainly when bronchial flow is already compromised, as in left heart failure. When it occurs, the infarct is hemorrhagic, wedge-shaped, and based on the pleura. Repeated small emboli over time can produce chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.

blocks.title: Using the A-a gradient
blocks.text: A 34-year-old woman on estrogen breathes room air at sea level. PaO2 is 65 mm Hg and PaCO2 is 30 mm Hg. Alveolar PO2 equals 0.21 times (760 minus 47) minus PaCO2 divided by 0.8. That is about 150 minus 37.5, or about 112 mm Hg. The A-a gradient is 112 minus 65, about 47 mm Hg, far above the normal of roughly 5 to 15 mm Hg in a young adult. The low PaCO2 shows she is hyperventilating, so pure hypoventilation cannot explain her hypoxemia. A widened gradient points to a gas exchange defect, here ventilation-perfusion mismatch from pulmonary embolism.

blocks.predict: Why does a moderate embolus to a lobar artery usually leave the lung tissue alive in a healthy young patient but cause a wedge-shaped infarct in a patient with left heart failure?
blocks.explain: In the healthy patient bronchial arterial flow and alveolar oxygen sustain the tissue; in left heart failure bronchial flow is reduced and pulmonary venous pressure is high, so the dual supply fails.
blocks.check: Compare with the paragraph on why most emboli do not cause infarction.

sections.title: Deep vein thrombosis and superficial thrombophlebitis

blocks.text: Venous thrombi form in low-flow, low-pressure vessels and are rich in red cells and fibrin (red thrombi), unlike platelet-rich arterial thrombi. They usually begin in the valve pockets of deep calf veins, where flow is slowest, and can propagate proximally. Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is explained by Virchow triad, and most patients have more than one element.

blocks.title: Virchow triad and deep vein thrombosis risk
rows: Slow flow lets activated factors accumulate and keeps platelets near the endothelium
Immobility, long travel, paralysis, heart failure, compression by the pregnant uterus
Loss of anticoagulant surface and exposure of tissue factor
Surgery and trauma, especially hip and knee; central venous catheters; prior DVT
Excess procoagulant or loss of natural anticoagulant
Factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antiphospholipid antibodies, malignancy, estrogen and pregnancy, nephrotic syndrome (urinary antithrombin loss)
blocks.caption: Major surgery and cancer are high-risk because they combine all three elements.

blocks.text: A DVT obstructs venous outflow, raising capillary hydrostatic pressure, while inflammation of the vein wall adds pain and warmth. The typical finding is one swollen, warm, tender leg, sometimes with dilated superficial veins and a calf circumference larger than the other side. Many DVTs are silent because collateral veins drain the limb, which is why pulmonary embolism may be the first sign. Calf pain on dorsiflexion (Homans sign) is unreliable. Proximal thrombi carry the greatest embolic risk (C07). On ultrasound the thrombosed vein cannot be compressed because clot fills its lumen.

Superficial thrombophlebitis is thrombosis with inflammation in a superficial vein, often a varicose vein or a vein used for an intravenous catheter. It produces a tender, red, palpable cord along the vein, with little limb swelling because deep drainage is intact, and it rarely embolizes unless it extends into the deep system. Migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau sign of malignancy) is recurrent superficial and deep venous thrombosis appearing and resolving at different sites. It occurs with adenocarcinomas, classically pancreatic and also lung, gastric, and colon, which release tissue factor and mucin that activate coagulation. This Trousseau sign must not be confused with the Trousseau sign of hypocalcemia (carpal spasm under a blood pressure cuff).

Superficial veins, often varicose or cannulated

Red, tender, palpable cord; little swelling

blocks.caption: The deep veins drain most of the leg, so their occlusion causes diffuse edema and embolic risk.

sections.title: Varicose veins and chronic venous insufficiency

blocks.text: Leg veins return blood against gravity using the calf muscle pump and one-way valves. During walking, calf contraction squeezes the deep veins, and competent valves let blood move only upward and from superficial to deep through perforating veins. This keeps standing venous pressure at the ankle low during movement. When valves fail, the column of blood is no longer interrupted, and pressure in the superficial veins stays high even with walking (ambulatory venous hypertension).

Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins, most often in the great saphenous system, produced by raised intraluminal pressure and weakness of the vein wall that make the valves incompetent. Risk rises with age, female sex, pregnancy (compression of the inferior vena cava by the uterus plus hormonal relaxation of the vein wall), obesity, prolonged standing, and family history. Prior DVT that damages deep valves causes secondary venous insufficiency. Superficial varicose veins rarely cause embolism. Varicosities can form elsewhere when pressure rises, such as esophageal varices and hemorrhoids in portal hypertension.

steps: Valve incompetence in superficial, perforating, or deep veins

blocks.caption: Chronic venous hypertension injures skin through edema, inflammation, and poor oxygen delivery.

blocks.text: Chronic venous insufficiency therefore produces edema that worsens through the day and improves with elevation, aching heaviness, brown pigmentation, itchy eczematous stasis dermatitis, and indurated skin around the lower leg. Ulcers form most often just above the medial malleolus, where pressure from incompetent perforators and the great saphenous system is highest. They are shallow, irregular, and moist, unlike arterial ulcers.

blocks.title: Venous versus arterial ulcers
rows: Toes, heel, pressure points, distal foot

blocks.caption: Elevation helps venous ulcers by lowering venous pressure but worsens arterial ischemia by lowering perfusion pressure.

blocks.text: Raynaud phenomenon is episodic, reversible vasospasm of the small arteries and arterioles of the fingers and toes, and sometimes the nose and ears, triggered by cold or emotional stress. Digital vessels normally constrict to cold through sympathetic alpha-adrenergic signaling, mainly alpha-2 receptors, to conserve core heat. In Raynaud phenomenon this response is exaggerated and the lumen closes completely.

blocks.title: Color sequence of a Raynaud attack
steps: Cold or stress: intense digital artery spasm
White: pallor from absent arterial inflow
Blue: cyanosis as stagnant blood is deoxygenated
Spasm relaxes on rewarming
Red: reactive hyperemia with throbbing and tingling
blocks.caption: The colors trace inflow stopping, oxygen being extracted from trapped blood, and inflow returning above baseline.

blocks.text: The red phase is reactive hyperemia: during ischemia, local metabolites such as adenosine, CO2, H+, and K+ accumulate and dilate the arterioles, so when the spasm lifts, flow rebounds well above normal. Not every attack shows all three colors, and pallor is the most specific.

Primary Raynaud phenomenon (Raynaud disease) is a functional disorder of vascular reactivity with no underlying disease, most common in young women, usually symmetric, and without tissue damage. Secondary Raynaud phenomenon results from structural or inflammatory disease of the vessels, so the lumen is already narrowed and spasm can cause ischemic injury. It is nearly universal in systemic sclerosis, where intimal proliferation narrows digital arteries, and occurs with lupus, thromboangiitis obliterans (C11), atherosclerosis, cryoglobulinemia, and repetitive use of vibrating tools. Signs that suggest secondary disease are onset after about 30 to 40, asymmetric attacks, digital pits or ulcers, abnormal dilated or dropped-out nailfold capillaries, and positive autoantibodies.

rows: Systemic sclerosis, lupus, Buerger disease, others
Young woman, onset in teens to twenties
Older onset, features of the underlying disease
blocks.caption: Tissue damage implies a structurally narrowed vessel, which points to secondary disease.

blocks.text: Thromboangiitis obliterans is a segmental, thrombosing, acute and chronic inflammation of medium and small arteries, mainly the tibial and radial arteries and their digital branches, that spreads secondarily to adjacent veins and nerves. It occurs almost exclusively in heavy smokers and classically begins before about age 35 to 40, more often in men. Tobacco exposure is central to the disease: the mechanism is thought to involve hypersensitivity or direct endothelial toxicity from tobacco products, and the disease rarely progresses once all tobacco use stops.

Microscopically, the involved segment shows a luminal thrombus containing microabscesses, small collections of neutrophils surrounded by granulomatous inflammation, with the internal elastic lamina relatively preserved. Over time the thrombus organizes and recanalizes, and the artery, vein, and nerve become bound together in fibrous tissue. Lesions are sharply segmental, with normal vessel between them, which separates the disease from the diffuse plaques of atherosclerosis.

The clinical features follow from distal small-vessel occlusion with nerve involvement. Early signs include cold sensitivity and Raynaud phenomenon, and nodular superficial phlebitis that migrates along veins. Claudication tends to involve the instep of the foot or the forearm and hand, because the disease is distal. Inflamed nerves add intense rest pain out of proportion to the visible lesion. Progressive occlusion leads to painful digital ulcers and gangrene, often needing amputation if smoking continues. Peripheral pulses at the wrist and ankle may be absent while proximal pulses are normal.

blocks.title: Buerger disease versus atherosclerotic PAD

Large and medium arteries of legs
Migratory superficial phlebitis, Raynaud, upper limb involvement, severe neural pain
Calf or buttock claudication; risk factors beyond smoking
blocks.caption: Distal arm and leg involvement in a young smoker with phlebitis suggests Buerger disease.

sections.title: Giant cell arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica

blocks.text: Vasculitis is inflammation of the vessel wall. The Chapel Hill classification groups the vasculitides by the size of vessel mainly affected, which predicts the clinical picture: large-vessel disease narrows the aorta and its branches and causes limb or organ ischemia; medium-vessel disease causes infarcts and aneurysms in organs; small-vessel disease involves capillaries and venules, producing palpable purpura, glomerulonephritis, and alveolar hemorrhage.

blocks.title: Vasculitis by vessel size
rows: T cell and antibody response to unknown trigger
Oral and genital ulcers, uveitis; HLA-B51
blocks.caption: Vessel size and immune mechanism together predict the organs involved and the laboratory findings.

blocks.text: Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also called temporal arteritis, is the most common vasculitis in older adults. It almost never begins before age 50, affects women more often, and is most frequent in people of Northern European ancestry. It is a T cell mediated granulomatous inflammation of large and medium arteries, mainly the branches of the external carotid artery (including the superficial temporal artery), the ophthalmic and posterior ciliary arteries, the vertebral arteries, and the aorta. Activated T cells and macrophages release cytokines including IL-6, which drives the acute-phase response.

Inflammation narrows the lumen, so symptoms are ischemic: new headache with a tender, thickened temporal artery; jaw claudication (pain on chewing from masseter ischemia); and visual loss from occlusion of the ophthalmic or posterior ciliary arteries, which causes anterior ischemic optic neuropathy and can produce sudden, permanent blindness. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate is markedly raised, often above 50 mm/h, with high CRP. Biopsy shows granulomatous inflammation of the inner media with multinucleated giant cells and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, but lesions are segmental (skip lesions), so a short or unlucky biopsy can be negative. Aortic involvement can later cause thoracic aneurysm.

Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is an inflammatory disorder of the same age group causing pain and morning stiffness of the shoulder and hip girdles and neck, with a high ESR but normal creatine kinase and normal strength, because the target is periarticular synovium and bursae rather than muscle. The two conditions overlap: about half of patients with GCA have PMR symptoms, and a smaller fraction of patients with PMR develop GCA.

Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis of large arteries, principally the aortic arch and its branches, and sometimes the descending and abdominal aorta, the renal arteries, and the pulmonary arteries. It most often affects women under about 40 to 50 and is more common in Asia. The histology resembles giant cell arteritis: mononuclear infiltrates, granulomas with giant cells, and destruction of the media. What separates the two is mainly age, so a granulomatous large-vessel arteritis in a young woman is Takayasu, and in a patient over 50 it is GCA.

Chronic inflammation is followed by fibrosis of the media and adventitia and thickening of the intima, giving an irregularly thickened aortic wall and stenosis or occlusion of the origins of the great vessels. The disease often begins with nonspecific constitutional symptoms (fever, fatigue, weight loss, arthralgia, raised ESR) before ischemic signs appear. Because the subclavian arteries are narrowed at their origins, pulses in one or both arms become weak or absent, giving the older name pulseless disease. Blood pressure measured in the affected arm is lower, so the two arms differ, and the patient may have arm claudication with use. Bruits are heard over the subclavian and carotid arteries.

Other findings follow the vessels involved. Carotid and vertebral narrowing causes dizziness, syncope, visual disturbances, and stroke. Renal artery stenosis activates the renin-angiotensin system and causes hypertension, which can be masked when it is measured in a narrowed arm. Involvement of the aortic root can dilate it and cause aortic regurgitation, and pulmonary artery involvement can cause pulmonary hypertension. Weak arm pulses with unequal pressures in a young woman should raise Takayasu arteritis, while the same finding with sudden tearing pain suggests aortic dissection (C05).

blocks.title: Giant cell arteritis versus Takayasu arteritis
rows: Headache, jaw claudication, vision loss, PMR
Weak arm pulses, unequal arm pressures, arm claudication, bruits
Granulomatous with giant cells, then fibrosis
blocks.caption: Both are granulomatous large-vessel vasculitides; age and the vessels involved separate them.

blocks.text: Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) is a systemic necrotizing vasculitis of small and medium muscular arteries, typically renal and visceral arteries, that spares the pulmonary arteries and does not involve arterioles, capillaries, or venules. Because the smallest vessels are spared, PAN does not cause glomerulonephritis. It most often affects young to middle-aged adults. A substantial minority of patients, historically about a third, have chronic hepatitis B infection, and in them immune complexes containing hepatitis B surface antigen deposit in the vessel wall (a type III mechanism). ANCA is characteristically negative.

The lesion is segmental transmural inflammation with fibrinoid necrosis of the wall, initially rich in neutrophils, eosinophils, and mononuclear cells. Necrosis weakens the wall, producing small aneurysms that give involved arteries a beaded or nodular appearance (the source of the name), and it promotes thrombosis and infarction. A hallmark is that acute lesions and healed, fibrotic lesions coexist in the same patient and even the same artery, showing that injury occurs in waves. Angiography of the renal or mesenteric arteries shows multiple microaneurysms and stenoses.

Manifestations reflect ischemia and infarction of the organs supplied. Renal artery involvement causes renal infarcts and renin-mediated hypertension, a leading cause of death. Mesenteric arteritis produces abdominal pain worse after meals, bleeding, and bowel infarction or perforation. Inflammation of the vasa nervorum produces mononeuritis multiplex, such as foot drop. Skin findings include painful nodules, livedo reticularis, and ulcers, and testicular pain can occur. Constitutional symptoms are common: fever, malaise, and weight loss.

blocks.title: Polyarteritis nodosa features explained
rows: Arteritis of renal and intrarenal arteries reduces glomerular perfusion and activates renin
Mesenteric arteritis with ischemia that worsens with digestive demand
Infarction of nerves through vasa nervorum involvement
Pulmonary arteries and small vessels spared
Fibrinoid necrosis weakens the wall at multiple points
blocks.caption: PAN is a medium-vessel disease, so it produces infarcts and aneurysms rather than capillary inflammation.

blocks.text: Kawasaki disease (mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome) is an acute, self-limited vasculitis of medium arteries that mainly affects children under 5 and is most common in children of East Asian, especially Japanese, ancestry. It is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries. The trigger is unknown; the leading view is that an infectious agent provokes an exaggerated T cell and antibody response in genetically susceptible children, with activated macrophages and cytokines damaging the vessel wall. The arteritis is transmural with mixed inflammatory cells, and fibrinoid necrosis is usually less prominent than in PAN.

The diagnosis is clinical. A child has fever lasting at least 5 days plus most of the five principal features listed below. The mucocutaneous findings reflect widespread inflammation of small and medium vessels and are temporary; peeling of the fingers and toes typically follows in the second to third week. Irritability is marked, and laboratory tests show raised ESR and CRP, leukocytosis, and, after the first week, thrombocytosis.

blocks.title: Principal features of Kawasaki disease
rows: High fever for 5 days or more
Bilateral nonexudative conjunctival injection, sparing the limbus
Red, cracked lips; strawberry tongue; diffuse oral redness
Polymorphous rash, often on trunk and perineum
Red, swollen hands and feet; later periungual desquamation
Cervical lymphadenopathy, usually unilateral, at least 1.5 cm
blocks.caption: Fever plus at least four of the five other features supports classic Kawasaki disease.

blocks.text: The key complication is coronary artery aneurysm, which develops in roughly a quarter of untreated children. Inflammation destroys the internal elastic lamina and media of the coronary arteries, which then dilate. Inside an aneurysm, flow is slow and turbulent, and the high platelet count adds to the tendency to thrombose, so coronary thrombosis can cause myocardial infarction or sudden death in a young child; aneurysms can also rupture, and healing can leave stenosis. Myocarditis, pericarditis, and valvular regurgitation can occur in the acute phase. Scarlet fever also gives a strawberry tongue and rash, but it is caused by group A streptococcal infection, usually with exudative pharyngitis, and does not cause conjunctivitis or coronary aneurysms.

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) target enzymes stored in neutrophil granules. PR3-ANCA (proteinase 3) gives a cytoplasmic pattern on immunofluorescence (c-ANCA), and MPO-ANCA (myeloperoxidase) gives a perinuclear pattern (p-ANCA). When infection or cytokines prime neutrophils, PR3 and MPO move to the cell surface, where ANCA bind them. Bound neutrophils degranulate and release reactive oxygen species while adhering to endothelium, injuring small vessels (arterioles, capillaries, venules). Because injury depends on activated cells rather than deposits, these diseases are pauci-immune: biopsies show little immunoglobulin or complement, unlike immune complex vasculitis.

The organs most affected are those rich in capillaries: the kidney, where necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis causes hematuria, red cell casts, and rapidly progressive renal failure; and the lung, where capillaritis causes alveolar hemorrhage and hemoptysis. Combined lung hemorrhage and glomerulonephritis is a pulmonary-renal syndrome, which also occurs with anti-GBM disease, where immunofluorescence instead shows linear IgG along the basement membrane.

blocks.title: Distinguishing the ANCA-associated vasculitides
rows: Chronic sinusitis, nasal ulcers, septal perforation, saddle nose, otitis
Classic triad: upper airway, lung, kidney
Like GPA without granulomas or upper airway disease
Blood eosinophilia, mononeuritis multiplex, cardiac involvement
blocks.caption: Granulomas, eosinophils, and the ANCA type separate the three diseases.

blocks.text: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) combines necrotizing granulomas of the upper and lower respiratory tract with small-vessel vasculitis and glomerulonephritis, so a patient with chronic bloody sinusitis, lung nodules or cavities, and hematuria fits the pattern. Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) has the same small-vessel injury in lung, kidney, and skin (palpable purpura) but no granulomas. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA, formerly Churg-Strauss syndrome) progresses from asthma and allergic rhinitis to blood and tissue eosinophilia and then vasculitis; eosinophil granule proteins contribute to injury, and cardiac involvement is the main cause of death. ANCA is positive in fewer than half of EGPA patients.

IgA vasculitis (formerly Henoch-Schonlein purpura) is the most common systemic vasculitis of childhood, typically between about 3 and 15 years, and often follows an upper respiratory infection. Patients have an excess of galactose-deficient IgA1, which is recognized by autoantibodies to form immune complexes that deposit in small vessels of the skin, gut, joints, and glomerular mesangium, where they activate complement through the alternative and lectin pathways. This is an immune complex (type III) mechanism, and immunofluorescence shows IgA in vessel walls and the mesangium.

The findings follow the sites of deposition. Dermal leukocytoclastic vasculitis produces palpable purpura over the buttocks and the extensor surfaces of the legs, where gravity and hydrostatic pressure favor deposition. Because the purpura comes from inflamed vessels, the platelet count and coagulation tests are normal, which separates it from thrombocytopenic purpura. Joint involvement causes arthralgia or arthritis, usually of the knees and ankles. Gut vasculitis causes colicky abdominal pain and bleeding and predisposes to intussusception, often ileoileal. Renal involvement is a mesangial glomerulonephritis identical to IgA nephropathy, presenting with hematuria and sometimes proteinuria; it is more often severe in adults.

Behcet syndrome is a variable-vessel vasculitis that can affect arteries and veins of any size. It is most common along the old Silk Road from the Mediterranean and Middle East to Japan and is associated with HLA-B51. Neutrophil hyperactivity drives recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers (nearly all patients), genital ulcers, and uveitis that can cause blindness, sometimes with a hypopyon. Skin lesions include erythema nodosum and pathergy, an exaggerated pustular response to a needle prick. Venous thrombosis, arterial aneurysms, and neurologic involvement add to its morbidity.

integration.text: Most vascular disease can be organized by which layer of the wall fails. Intimal disease (atherosclerosis) narrows the lumen and seeds thrombi and emboli. Medial disease weakens the wall: atherosclerotic starvation of the media, cystic medial degeneration in Marfan syndrome, syphilitic endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, and fibrinoid necrosis in PAN all lead to aneurysm or dissection, and the law of Laplace explains why dilation, once started, tends to progress. Biochemistry supplies the lipid side of the story through the LDL receptor and PCSK9, microbiology supplies syphilis, Salmonella, and hepatitis B, and hemostasis explains venous thrombosis through Virchow triad.

Immunology explains the vasculitides better than memorized lists. T cell granulomatous inflammation (GCA, Takayasu) targets large arteries and causes stenosis; immune complexes (hepatitis B associated PAN, IgA vasculitis) and ANCA-activated neutrophils (GPA, MPA, EGPA) injure medium and small vessels, with immunofluorescence separating deposit-rich from pauci-immune disease. Vessel size then predicts the clinical picture: pulse loss and claudication for large vessels, infarcts and microaneurysms for medium vessels, and purpura, glomerulonephritis, and alveolar hemorrhage for small vessels. The main limit of this scheme is overlap, since Kawasaki disease and PAN can involve smaller vessels and Behcet syndrome affects vessels of every size.

summary: Atherosclerosis is intimal and narrows the lumen; arteriolosclerosis narrows arterioles (hyaline with diabetes and hypertension, hyperplastic onion-skin with severe hypertension); Monckeberg calcifies the media without narrowing the lumen.
Atherogenesis runs from endothelial dysfunction through oxidized LDL, foam cells, and fatty streaks to a fibrous cap over a necrotic core; thin-capped plaques rupture and thrombose.
Familial hypercholesterolemia reduces LDL receptor clearance, so LDL rises in proportion to gene dosage and deposits in arteries, tendons, eyelids, and cornea.

Abdominal aortic aneurysms are infrarenal and atherosclerotic; thoracic aneurysms reflect cystic medial degeneration or syphilis; wall stress rises with radius, so large aneurysms expand and rupture faster.
Aortic dissection splits a weakened media under high pressure; Stanford A involves the ascending aorta and threatens tamponade, aortic regurgitation, and coronary occlusion.
Claudication reflects a fixed stenosis that cannot raise flow with exercise; an ABI of 0.90 or lower confirms PAD, while cholesterol emboli cause blue toes with intact pulses.
Pulmonary emboli come mainly from proximal leg DVT and cause hypoxemia with a widened A-a gradient through V/Q mismatch; the bronchial supply prevents infarction in most cases.
Virchow triad explains DVT risk; superficial thrombophlebitis is a tender cord with little embolic risk, and migratory thrombophlebitis signals visceral adenocarcinoma.
Incompetent venous valves produce ambulatory venous hypertension, edema, hemosiderin staining, stasis dermatitis, and ulcers above the medial malleolus.
Vessel size organizes vasculitis: GCA and Takayasu (large, granulomatous), PAN and Kawasaki (medium, aneurysms), ANCA and IgA vasculitis (small, purpura and glomerulonephritis).
